summary:
Pays de la Loire stands under the French national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal procedure, custodial oversight and marriage applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and the sources document no regional deviation material enough to assess separately. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Custody is the principal exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose identity documents record male sex — the vast majority, who have not had sex-reassignment surgery — are placed in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee describing inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence, and quotes Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, stating that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison; the feature illustrates this with the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions Hazan called worrying.

Placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, with each establishment improvising: special units, or isolation restricting contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between facilities, and the accounts collected in the 2018 feature describe heightened vulnerability to assault and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority and preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records the persistence of serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees in adult prisons, while noting that none were identified in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. None of those establishments lies in Pays de la Loire, so no inspection finding specific to this region is on the record.

The 2021 opinion found no marked improvement since 2010 despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The custodial findings divide sharply by setting: the CGLPL's 2021 review recorded serious violations in adult prisons and none in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. A trans visitor's exposure therefore turns on whether custody arises at all, and in which type of facility.

The 2016 legal gender-recognition reform did not translate into changed outcomes on the ground; the inspection authority recorded no marked improvement between its 2010 and 2021 opinions. Reform of the document regime and reform of placement practice are separate questions in France.

Risk concentrates in two settings, detention and the border, while the discrimination recorded by the Défenseur des droits and the EU Fundamental Rights Agency concerns services, accommodation and public movement — an environment of persistent mistreatment rather than criminal liability.

Named establishments in the inspection record — Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses — sit outside Pays de la Loire, as does the Tarbes prison holding Louna. The regional picture is carried by national findings and national mechanisms rather than by local inspections.

Residents held in places of deprivation of liberty in Pays de la Loire are covered by the binding guidance the CGLPL issued on 25 May 2021 for places of deprivation of liberty, which addresses placement by birth sex, isolation of vulnerable detainees, exposure during strip searches and suicide prevention.

Placement in prisons in the region follows Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code and the gender recorded on identity documents, with each establishment deciding its own arrangements between special units and isolation. The inspection authority's findings on that practice apply to adult prisons nationally.

Residents may access the 2016 legal gender-recognition procedure and, since the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013, full partner recognition. The Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights sets out guidance binding in effect on service providers, drawn from case files and association testimony.

Detained trans people in the region feed the national oversight bodies directly: the CGLPL's 2021 review drew on roughly forty referrals and a decade of letters from detained trans people, and its predecessor opinion of 30 June 2010 was followed up for the same reason.
